text: Here is an array of nine integers, some positive and some negative.
We want the contiguous run of numbers with the largest sum.
We will track a running sum as we scan left to right.
Whenever that running sum turns negative, we reset it to zero.
And we keep a best so far, the largest sum seen yet.
Add negative two: the running sum becomes negative two.
That is negative, so we drop the running sum back to zero.
Add one: the running sum climbs to one.
One beats our old best of zero, so best so far moves up.
Add negative three: the running sum drops to negative two.
Negative again, so the running sum resets to zero once more.
Add four: the running sum jumps up to four.
Four beats one, so best so far climbs to four.
Add negative one: the running sum eases down to three.
Add two: the running sum rises again, up to five.
Five beats four, so best so far climbs once more.
Add one more, and the running sum reaches six.
Six is our best yet, so the marker rises to match.
Add negative five: the running sum falls all the way to one.
Add four: the running sum ends at five, just short of six.
We have scanned every number, and best so far stops at six.
That six came from four, negative one, two, and one.
Four minus one plus two plus one really does add to six.
Notice we only swept across the array one single time.
One pass over n numbers means this algorithm runs in linear time.
Checking every possible subarray instead would cost order n squared.
One running sum, one number that only climbs, and the answer appears.
